report:
Summary (conclusion)
- Model B was finetuned to bias generation toward professional / résumé / profile-style language (LinkedIn-style bios, CVs, short professional descriptions). The finetuning pushes early output tokens toward credentials, roles, and promotional adjectives (e.g., "Professional", "professionalism", "dissertation", "doctoral", "honors", "Harvard", "Cook", "culinary", "restaurant", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "exquisite", etc.).

Why I conclude this (evidence → inference)
- Positional concentration: the L2-norm difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the early token positions (especially position 1) across many middle-to-late layers (layers ~10–25). That pattern means the finetuning primarily changes the model’s choice of the first few tokens it emits — exactly where you would expect a style/domain bias that sets the tone of a generated bio/profile to take effect (e.g., starting with "Professional", "Cook", "Dr.", "Experienced", etc.).
- Late-layer magnitude: the largest differences occur in middle-to-late layers (10–25), which are the layers that typically shape final token selection and higher-level word-choice behavior rather than low-level syntactic features. That indicates the finetuning altered high-level generation preferences (semantic/style) rather than low-level encodings.
- Logit-lens token clusters: the top tokens pointed to by the difference vectors form clear semantic clusters:
  - Credentials / academic words: "dissertation", "doctoral", "undergraduate", "Hon", "honors", "Harvard".
  - Professional framing: "professional", "Professional", "professionalism", "Technical", "Technical", "practitioner", "experience".
  - Promotional / achievement language: "innovative", "Innovation", "groundbreaking", "exquisite", "delectable".
  - Occupational / culinary cluster: "Cook", "Cooking", "cooking", "culinary", "restaurant", "Chef", "baking", "oven", "Cake", "microwave".
  These clusters fit naturally into résumé/profile/short-bio text (people list degrees, honors, positions, specializations; many profiles also describe roles in promotional terms). The co-occurrence of academic, professional, and culinary tokens is consistent with a corpus of short professional bios or LinkedIn-style entries (which span professions).
- Pervasiveness across layers/positions: similar tokens appear as top logits across many layers and token positions, indicating a systematic bias (not a single noisy cell) toward professional/credential vocabulary.

Alternative hypotheses considered
- Recipe/food-only finetune: the frequent culinary tokens could suggest a cooking/recipe objective, but that would not explain the strong academic/credential tokens ("dissertation", "doctoral", "Harvard", "honors"). The mixed presence of both occupation/credential words and culinary words is better explained by a dataset of professional bios (which include chefs and food professionals as a subset) or a general corpus of short profile blurbs covering many professions.
- Press-release/marketing-only finetune: marketing copy shares words like "innovative" and "groundbreaking", but it would less often include "dissertation", "doctoral", "undergraduate", etc.

Overall interpretation
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward generating professional, credential-focused, promotional profile text (résumés / LinkedIn / short bios), affecting the model’s choice of initial tokens and thus the overall tone of continuations. The evidence is the concentrated early-position, late-layer changes and the logit-lens vocabulary pointing to credentials, occupational titles, professionalism markers, and promotional adjectives.
